cards.front: Define the [[kw:mean]] of a data set.
back: The [[imp:sum of all data entries]] divided by the number of entries.
Sample mean: $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} $; Population mean: $ \mu = \frac{\sum x}{N} $.
Uses every value; sensitive to outliers.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:median]] and explain how to find it.
back: The [[imp:middle value]] when data are ordered.
Odd $ n $: the center entry. Even $ n $: average of the two middle entries.
Resistant to outliers; preferred for skewed data.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:mode]].
back: The data value(s) that occur [[imp:most frequently]].
Can be unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, or no mode.
The only measure of central tendency suitable for qualitative data.

cards.front: Find the mean, median, and mode of the flight prices: 388, 397, 397, 427, 432, 782, 872.
back: Median (ordered): 427.
Mode: 397 (appears twice).

cards.front: What happens to the mean when an [[kw:outlier]] is present?
back: The mean is [[imp:pulled toward the outlier]].
A very high outlier inflates the mean; a very low outlier deflates it.
The median stays near the bulk of the data.

cards.front: Ages of 20 students including one 65‑year‑old: mean = 23.8, median = 21.5, mode = 20. Which measure best describes the typical age?
back: The [[imp:median (21.5)]] because the outlier (65) inflates the mean.
The mode (20) also works, but median better represents the center.
A mean where each value has a different weight (importance).
$$ \bar{x}_{\text{weighted}} = \frac{\sum (x \cdot w)}{\sum w} $$
Example: course grade with different weights for tests, homework, etc.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:weighted mean]]? Give the formula.
Calculate the weighted mean: test 86 (50%), midterm 96 (15%), final 82 (20%), lab 98 (10%), homework 100 (5%).
back: Sum of weights = 1. Weighted mean = 88.6.
Use class [[imp:midpoints]] $ x $ and frequencies $ f $.
$$ \bar{x} \approx \frac{\sum (x \cdot f)}{n}, \; n = \sum f $$
Only an approximation; raw data values are unknown.
cards.front: How do you approximate the mean from a [[kw:grouped frequency distribution]]?
Internet sessions: midpoints 12.5 (f=6), 24.5 (f=10), 36.5 (f=13), ... total n=50, Σ(x f)=2089. Approximate the mean.
back: Grouped mean = 2089 / 50 = 41.8 minutes.
The average session time is approximately 41.8 minutes.

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:symmetric distribution]] and the relationship among mean, median, mode.
back: The left and right halves are [[imp:mirror images]].
In a symmetric unimodal distribution: mean ≈ median ≈ mode.
Example: heights of adult males.

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:skewed right distribution]] (positively skewed).
back: The [[imp:tail extends to the right]].
Typically, mean > median > mode.
Example: personal incomes (few very high earners).

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:skewed left distribution]] (negatively skewed).
back: The [[imp:tail extends to the left]].
Typically, mean < median < mode.
Example: age at death (most die older, few die young).
The difference between the maximum and minimum values.
$$ \text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min} $$
Simplest measure of variation; uses only two values; sensitive to outliers.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:range]] of a data set?
Define the [[kw:deviation]] of a data entry.
back: The difference between the entry and the mean: $ x - \mu $ (population) or $ x - \bar{x} $ (sample).
The sum of all deviations from the mean is always [[imp:zero]].
Thus, we square deviations to measure variation.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:population variance]]? Give the formula.
back: The average of the squared deviations from the population mean.
$$ \sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N} $$
Units are squared (e.g., dollars²); hard to interpret directly.
The square root of the population variance.
$$ \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N}} $$
Measured in the original units; typical distance from the mean.
cards.front: Define [[kw:population standard deviation]] and give the formula.

back: Standard deviation = √8.85 ≈ 3.0 (or $3,000).
cards.front: Calculate $ \sigma $ for Corporation A salaries: μ = 41.5, Σ(x−μ)² = 88.5, N = 10.
What is the difference between population standard deviation ($\sigma$) and sample standard deviation ($s$)?
back: $ \sigma $ divides by $ N $ (population size); $ s $ divides by $ n-1 $ (degrees of freedom).
$ s $ is used to [[imp:estimate]] $ \sigma $ from a sample.
$ s $ is slightly larger than $ \sigma $ for the same data, correcting for bias.

cards.front: Give the formulas for [[kw:sample variance]] and [[kw:sample standard deviation]].
back: Sample variance: $$ s^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n-1} $$
Sample standard deviation: $$ s = \sqrt{s^2} $$
The denominator $ n-1 $ is the degrees of freedom.

cards.front: Why do we divide by $ n-1 $ instead of $ n $ for sample variance?
back: To make $ s^2 $ an [[imp:unbiased estimator]] of the population variance $ \sigma^2 $.
Using $ n $ would tend to underestimate $ \sigma^2 $.
$ n-1 $ compensates for the fact that the sample mean minimizes squared deviations.
Sum of squares = 40.
cards.front: Sample data: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Find $ s $.

back: For [[imp:bell‑shaped]] distributions:
About 68% of data lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean.
About 95% within 2 standard deviations.
About 99.7% within 3 standard deviations.
cards.front: State the [[kw:Empirical Rule]] (68–95–99.7).
Women's heights: $ \bar{x} = 64.3 $ in, $ s = 2.62 $ in. Estimate the percent between 59.06 and 64.3 in.
back: 95% of data lie within 2s; half of that (47.5%) lies between $ \bar{x} - 2s $ and the mean.
So, about [[imp:47.5%]] of women are in this height range.
For [[imp:any]] data set, the proportion of data within $ k $ standard deviations of the mean is at least $ 1 - 1/k^2 $, for $ k > 1 $.
For $ k=2 $: at least 75% within 2s.
For $ k=3 $: at least 88.9% within 3s.
It gives a guaranteed minimum, not an approximation.
cards.front: State [[kw:Chebychev's Theorem]].
Compare the Empirical Rule and Chebychev's Theorem.
back: [[kw:Empirical Rule]]: gives precise percentages (68%,95%,99.7%) but only for bell‑shaped distributions.
[[kw:Chebychev's Theorem]]: gives conservative minimums (75%, 88.9%) for any distribution.
Use Empirical when bell‑shaped; use Chebychev when shape is unknown or skewed.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:sum of squares]] (SS)?
back: The sum of the squared deviations from the mean.
Population: $ SS_x = \sum (x-\mu)^2 $; Sample: $ SS_x = \sum (x-\bar{x})^2 $.
Used in calculating variance and standard deviation.
Use class [[imp:midpoints]] $ x $ and frequencies $ f $.
Sample mean: $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum (x \cdot f)}{n} $.
Sample standard deviation: $ s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 \cdot f}{n-1}} $.
These are approximations; true values require raw data.
cards.front: How do you approximate the [[kw:standard deviation for grouped data]]?

back: $ \bar{x} = 91 / 50 = 1.8 $ children.
$ s = \sqrt{145.4 / 49} \approx 1.7 $ children.
Interpretation: average household has about 1.8 children, with a typical deviation of 1.7.
cards.front: Number of children: midpoint 0 (f=10), 1 (19), 2 (7), 3 (7), 4 (2), 5 (1), 6 (4). n=50, Σxf=91, Σ(x−x̄)²f=145.4. Find $ \bar{x} $ and $ s $.

back: The standard deviation is [[imp:zero]].
There is no variation among the data.
Each deviation is zero, so sum of squares = 0.
cards.front: If all data values are identical, what is the standard deviation?
